title: Crossing or rubbing stems — what to do once confirmed

common.preserved_uncertainty: Only 2 of about 16 sources give any rule for which of the two stems to remove (AF-7, Low), so Pip gives none. The Kansas City Rose Society allows cutting back to the next outward-facing bud instead of a full cut (shown). One source argues against deliberately opening the centre of the bush (C-1, unresolved). Whether a gardener should wait when unsure which stem to remove was not addressed by any source (AF-8).

decision_notes.text: Where two stems cross or rub, remove one of them as part of ordinary pruning.

Cut the stem you remove back to the bud union (the swollen join near the base) or to the larger cane it grows from, rather than just shortening it. One source also allows cutting it back to the next outward-facing bud.
When you shorten a cane, cut just above a bud that faces outward, so the new shoot grows away from the centre of the bush.
Why: stems rubbing together damage each other's canes, which lets disease in.
Take care not to damage the stem you're keeping; cut a tangled stem out in sections rather than pulling it whole.
